title: Weak contractibility of filtered ordinary nerves
statement: Let $I$ be a small ordinary category and let $N(I)$ be its simplicial nerve, with weak contractibility as defined in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Suppose $I$ is nonempty, any two objects $i,j$ admit arrows $i\to k$ and $j\to k$ to a common object, and every parallel pair $f,g:i\to j$ is coequalized by an arrow $h:j\to k$ with $hf=hg$. Then $N(I)\to\Delta^0$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. The dual assertion holds when common successors and coequalizers are replaced by common predecessors and equalizers; thus the nerve of any small nonempty cofiltered ordinary category is weakly contractible.

source.place: Tag 04AZ, definition-codirected, for the ordinary cofiltered hypotheses ONLY, and its opposite filtered convention. The weak-contractibility theorem is additional agent-formulated topology. WANTED: archived Kerodon, Proposition 9.1.1.17 and the comparison of ordinary filtered categories with filtered nerves. The ordinary-category comparison is Kerodon Corollary 9.1.2.8 (Tag 02PV), checked online along with Proposition 9.1.1.17 (Tag 02PH).

proof.text: Use the nerve and realization conventions of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Fix a finite simplicial subset $A\subseteq N(I)$, meaning finitely many nondegenerate simplices. Its set $V$ of vertices and set $E$ of nonidentity edges are finite. Choose a common target $k_0$ and arrows $v\to k_0$ for every $v\in V$: start with any object of $I$ and adjoin the finitely many vertices one at a time using the common-successor hypothesis, postcomposing the previously chosen arrows. Now enumerate $E$. Maintain a target $k$ and arrows $u_v:v\to k$ satisfying $u_w\circ e=u_v$ for the edges $e:v\to w$ already processed. At the next edge the arrows $u_w\circ e,u_v:v\to k$ are parallel. Choose $h:k\to k^{\prime}$ coequalizing them and replace every $u_v$ by $h\circ u_v$. This imposes the new equality and preserves all preceding equalities by associativity. Finite induction gives arrows $u_v:v\to k$ compatible with every edge of $A$; identity edges satisfy the equality automatically. If $A$ is empty, simply choose an object $k$ using nonemptiness.

source.place: Tag 04AZ, definition-codirected, opposite convention; agent finite-induction expansion of the three hypotheses, not an appeal to a theorem about nerves

proof.text:
Construct an actual contraction of the inclusion $|A|\to|N(I)|$. For a simplex $\sigma=(i_0\xrightarrow{f_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{f_n}i_n)$ of $A$ and barycentric coordinates $a=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, set
$$H([\sigma,a],t)=[(i_0\xrightarrow{f_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{f_n}i_n\xrightarrow{u_{i_n}}k),((1-t)a_0,\ldots,(1-t)a_n,t)].$$
Deleting an initial or internal vertex commutes with this formula by composition in $I$. Deleting the final vertex of $\sigma$ commutes because $u_{i_n}\circ f_n=u_{i_{n-1}}$, proved in step 1. Repeated vertices insert identities, so degeneracy identifications commute too. Thus the formula respects every generator of the realization equivalence relation in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. On each simplex times the interval the formula is continuous in the barycentric coordinates. The realization projection $\coprod_{n,\sigma\in A_n}|\Delta^n|\to|A|$ is a quotient map by definition. Apply [lem-cbc-quotient-cylinder-continuity] with this projection and $T=[0,1]$ (the usual closed real interval is locally compact; its neighborhoods contain closed subinterval neighborhoods). Continuity of the pullback is precisely continuity on each summand. Therefore $H$ is continuous jointly in both variables, with $H(-,0)$ the inclusion and $H(-,1)$ constant at $k$. The construction contracts the inclusion, and makes no claim that $A$ itself is contractible.

source.place: Proof opening choice independence; agent explicit barycentric contraction of a finite nerve piece, with quotient-cylinder continuity

proof.text: The realization is nonempty because any object of $I$ is a vertex. Every point $[\sigma,a]$ has a path to a vertex of $\sigma$, by linear interpolation of its barycentric coordinates to that vertex. For two vertices $i,j$, choose arrows $i\to k$ and $j\to k$ as in the hypothesis; their realized edges give paths from both vertices to $k$. Hence $|N(I)|$ is path connected, so its map to a point induces a bijection on components, in the sense of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones].

source.place: Proof opening choice independence; agent nonemptiness and component calculation

proof.text: Fix any basepoint $x\in|N(I)|$, an integer $n\geq1$, and a based continuous map $a:(S^n,s_0)\to(|N(I)|,x)$. By [lem-cbc-realization-compact-finite-support], $a$ factors continuously through $|A|$ for a finite simplicial subset $A$. Composing with step 2 gives a continuous homotopy $G:S^n\times[0,1]\to|N(I)|$ from $a$ to the constant map at $k$. To obtain a based nullhomotopy without assuming the apex equals $x$, extend $a$ to the closed unit ball by $F(rs)=G(s,1-r)$ for $0<r\leq1$ and $F(0)=k$. This is continuous away from zero. For an open neighborhood $U$ of $k$, the open set $G^{-1}(U)$ contains $S^n\times\{1\}$; using compactness of $S^n$ (included in the cited finite-support statement), finitely many product neighborhoods give $\varepsilon>0$ with $G(S^n\times(1-\varepsilon,1])\subseteq U$. Hence $F$ is continuous at zero as well. The formula $B(s,t)=F((1-t)s+t s_0)$ is now a continuous nullhomotopy of $a$ fixing $s_0$, since the ball is convex and $F(s_0)=a(s_0)=x$. Thus every based homotopy group vanishes. Together with step 3, the definition of weak homotopy equivalence in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones] proves $N(I)\to\Delta^0$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.

source.place: Proof opening choice independence; agent compact finite support and explicit based sphere contraction through a ball

proof.text: If $I$ satisfies the dual hypotheses, its opposite $I^{\mathrm{op}}$ satisfies exactly the three filtered hypotheses already treated. There is a homeomorphism $R:|N(I)|\to|N(I^{\mathrm{op}})|$ sending a chain $i_0\to\cdots\to i_n$ with coordinates $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ to the reversed opposite chain $i_n\to\cdots\to i_0$ with coordinates $(a_n,\ldots,a_0)$. Write $r_n$ for reversal of an $n$-chain and $\rho_n(a_0,\ldots,a_n)=(a_n,\ldots,a_0)$. For $n\geq1$ and $0\leq j\leq n$, deletion or composition at position $j$ gives $r_{n-1}d_j=d_{n-j}r_n$. For $n\geq0$ and $0\leq j\leq n$, duplicating vertex $j$ gives $r_{n+1}s_j=s_{n-j}r_n$. On coordinates, $\rho_n\delta_j=\delta_{n-j}\rho_{n-1}$ for insertion of a zero, and $\rho_n\sigma_j=\sigma_{n-j}\rho_{n+1}$ for addition of adjacent coordinates. These four identities respect the face and degeneracy relations defining the quotient in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], so $R$ is well defined. Each $\rho_n$ is continuous, hence the quotient topology makes $R$ continuous; reversing twice is the identity, giving a homeomorphism. For any two points $x,y$, compose a path from $R(x)$ to $R(y)$ with $R^{-1}$. For a based sphere map $a$ at $x$, apply the filtered case to $R\circ a$ based at $R(x)$ and compose its based nullhomotopy with $R^{-1}$; this fixes $x$ throughout. Thus the realization of $N(I)$ is path connected and every based homotopy group vanishes. This proves the cofiltered assertion. No simplicial isomorphism between the two nerves is asserted.
